items.text: Nested loops are a loop inside the body of another loop: the outer loop and the inner loop.
Because loops are statements, one can be the body of another; the inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

Outer init; outer test; [inner init; inner test; inner body; inner update; ... until the inner test fails]; rest of the outer body; outer update; outer test; ... The inner init runs again on every outer pass.
The inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times: two loops of 1..10 call printf 100 times; DivisorPattern 3 prints 3 rows of 3 entries, each row ending with its row number.
One outer pass resets the inner variable, runs the complete inner loop, executes the rest of the outer body once, and then updates the outer variable once.
Usually both loops are for loops: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j; matrix multiplication adds a third, innermost loop over k for each dot product.
A plain break ends only the innermost loop; a labeled break is needed when the inner loop must end the outer one too.
Which loop is outside decides the visiting order: row index outside gives row-major order, column index outside gives column-major order.
Plan: process every pair (i, j) - two-dimensional tables, every row x column of a matrix, every pair of elements; the outer variable is a slow stepper, the inner a fast stepper.

Swapping the outer and inner loops visits the same pairs in a different order (rows vs columns), which preserves a sum but changes printed layout; moving a statement between the inner body and the outer body changes its count from (outer x inner) to outer.

Use nested loops when the work ranges over all combinations of two indices (tables, matrices, pairs); expect running time proportional to the product of the pass counts, and prefer a single loop when the second index is a function of the first.

Nested loops are a loop inside the body of another loop: the outer loop and the inner loop.
Because loops are statements, one can be the body of another; the inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

Outer init; outer test; [inner init; inner test; inner body; inner update; ... until the inner test fails]; rest of the outer body; outer update; outer test; ... The inner init runs again on every outer pass.
The inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times: two loops of 1..10 call printf 100 times; DivisorPattern 3 prints 3 rows of 3 entries, each row ending with its row number.
One outer pass resets the inner variable, runs the complete inner loop, executes the rest of the outer body once, and then updates the outer variable once.
Usually both loops are for loops: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j; matrix multiplication adds a third, innermost loop over k for each dot product.
A plain break ends only the innermost loop; a labeled break is needed when the inner loop must end the outer one too.
Which loop is outside decides the visiting order: row index outside gives row-major order, column index outside gives column-major order.
Plan: process every pair (i, j) - two-dimensional tables, every row x column of a matrix, every pair of elements; the outer variable is a slow stepper, the inner a fast stepper.

Swapping the outer and inner loops visits the same pairs in a different order (rows vs columns), which preserves a sum but changes printed layout; moving a statement between the inner body and the outer body changes its count from (outer x inner) to outer.

Use nested loops when the work ranges over all combinations of two indices (tables, matrices, pairs); expect running time proportional to the product of the pass counts, and prefer a single loop when the second index is a function of the first.

double is a primitive data type: Java's 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point type for representing real numbers.

Values are 64-bit IEEE 754 numbers (about 15 significant digits) plus the special values Infinity and NaN; +, -, *, / (and %) are defined; if at least one operand of a binary arithmetic operator is double, the operation is a floating-point operation.

Operators are applied in precedence order, left operand first; at each operator, if one operand is double the other is widened to double before the operation, and the result is rounded to the nearest double before the next operator uses it.
The result has type double: 5.0/3.0 is 1.6666666666666667, 10/3.0 is 3.3333333333333335, 1.0/0.0 is Infinity, Math.sqrt(-1.0) is NaN; println always shows a decimal part (3.0, not 3).

An assignment to a double variable stores the nearest representable value (x = x + 0.1 replaces x with the rounded sum); no double operation throws an exception, so the variable may end up holding Infinity or NaN.

Type flow decides the division: with two int operands a / b discards the fraction (10/3 is 3, and double d = 10/3; stores 3.0); if either operand is double the other is promoted and the fraction is kept (10/3.0 is 3.3333333333333335).
double and boolean never convert into each other (no cast is allowed either way); they meet only through comparisons, which take doubles and produce a boolean, e.g. (x < 3.1).

Every double operation rounds its result to the nearest representable value, so double results carry rounding error that can accumulate; this is why == on computed doubles is unreliable.
For double operands a zero divisor is not an error: 1.0/0.0 is Infinity, -1.0/0.0 is -Infinity and 0.0/0.0 is NaN, whereas int division by zero throws an exception.
double is one of the eight primitive types and the default type of decimal literals (float would need an f suffix and is not used in the book).

The left operand is evaluated fully, then the right operand, and then the operator is applied in the promoted type.

Each / is evaluated when its turn comes (precedence, then left to right), using the types of its own two operands. Promoting the result to double, by a cast or by assignment, happens only afterwards and cannot restore the lost fraction.
